## 2. Policy context

A newspaper has reported that the Mayor’s social mobility adviser owns
three homes and lists two on Airbnb, including one that remains
council-owned. The opposition proposes requiring professional landlords
to register their properties and face higher Council Tax rates.

## 3. Is Airbnb “out of control” in London?

[W7 draft. Define what would count as evidence of a problem. Start with
a borough-level table or ranked bar chart of entire-home listings.
If comparable housing stock data are available, map entire-home listings
per 1,000 dwellings to show their local scale. Use a line chart if there
are comparable snapshots to show change over time.]

## 4. How many professional landlords are there?

[W8 draft. Use host IDs to count the number of hosts under a proposed
definition. For discussion, compare hosts with at least two entire-home
listings in London against those with at least three. Explain why the
thresholds are plausible and what a platform host ID can tell us about
property ownership.]

## 5. How many properties could the proposal affect?

[W9 draft. Apply the Q2 definitions to the listing data and count the
distinct listings that would fall within scope under each scenario.
Agree whether to count every listing linked to a qualifying host or
only their entire-home listings. State any limits to treating listing
counts as property counts.]

## 6. What are the likely benefits and drawbacks?

[Compare the implications for the Mayor, residents and the city.
Discuss registration and higher Council Tax separately, since each
has different effects and implementation requirements. Everyone can
draft a paragraph. Combine the strongest arguments next week.]

## 7. Can the story be reframed around social mobility or housing opportunity?
